analysis.one_liner: Bans smoking on all scheduled domestic flights, phasing in over three years.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote, but the shorter-flight smoking ban it built on became law later in 1989 through a different aviation bill.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made permanent the existing ban on smoking on domestic flights of two hours or less, and then extended it year by year: flights of three hours or less in 1990, and four hours or less in 1991 [S3]. It would have made smoking illegal in the passenger cabin and lavatories on any scheduled airline flight in US air transportation [S3]. The bill was sent to the House Public Works and Transportation Committee, went to its Aviation Subcommittee, held a hearing, and then the record simply points to another bill, H.R. 3015 [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Passengers and flight crews. Non-smoking travelers no longer breathe secondhand smoke on flights, and flight attendants, who work in the cabin all day, are the most exposed workers. At the time, flight attendant unions were among the loudest voices for cabin smoking bans.

how_it_helps.text: Makes smoking unlawful in the passenger cabin and lavatory on every scheduled domestic airline flight, starting with flights of two hours or less in 1989 [S3].
Phases in the ban to cover flights of three hours or less in 1990 and four hours or less in 1991, so longer flights are covered as the rule matures [S3].
Makes the two-hour ban permanent by writing it into the Federal Aviation Act, rather than leaving it as a temporary rule [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Smokers lose the ability to smoke on domestic flights. Tobacco companies lose a space where they had a captive adult audience and their products were in constant use. Airlines take on modest costs to enforce the rule and handle passengers who violate it.

drawbacks.text: Smokers who cannot abstain for a long flight face an uncomfortable situation, and the bill relies on enforcement by airline crews rather than accommodating smokers in any way [S3].
The phase-in is slow by design: even in 1991, flights longer than four hours would still allow smoking, so transcontinental and international passengers would not be protected under this bill [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and comfort gains for the traveling public and cabin crews are large and well established, while the costs fall on smokers' personal choices and on tobacco companies' market. The main design weakness is the narrow phase-in, which leaves the longest flights unprotected even at full effect.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Transportation Committee's Aviation Subcommittee, held one hearing, and was then set aside in favor of a broader aviation bill, H.R. 3015, without ever reaching the House floor.

narrative.text: Introduced February 2, 1989 by Rep. James Scheuer with no cosponsors [S4].
Referred to the House Committee on Public Works and Transportation, then to the Aviation Subcommittee on February 16, 1989 [S5].
The subcommittee held a hearing on June 22, 1989, and no further action followed [S5].
On November 21, 1989, the record notes 'See H.R.3015', indicating the measure was taken up in that broader aviation bill [S5].

A smoking ban covering domestic flights of two hours or less was enacted into law in late 1989 through separate aviation legislation, and was later extended to more flights — widely reported and well known, though not in the provided sources.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Travelers and flight attendants came out ahead, because the substance of the ban became law through other vehicles even though this bill itself died in committee. Tobacco companies were better off than under the full four-hour version, since the enacted rules were narrower.

for.name: Rep. James H. Scheuer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend and make permanent the flight smoking ban

for.name: Flight attendant unions
for.role: Cabin crew unions (notably the Association of Flight Attendants)
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned for ending smoking on airline flights, arguing their members were exposed to secondhand smoke all day at work

against.name: Tobacco companies
against.role: Cigarette manufacturers and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against cabin smoking bans and funded pro-smoking-rights campaigns during this period

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes were taken on this bill, so the partisan shape of support and opposition cannot be measured from the record; the sponsor was a Democrat with no cosponsors listed [S4].

industries.note: The bill removes one of the few places where cigarette makers' products are used continuously in front of a captive adult audience and shrinks the market for in-flight smoking. Ordinary passengers gain clean air at tobacco companies' expense.

Airlines would bear modest enforcement costs and some customer friction, but cabin smoking rules imposed uniformly also spare airlines from choosing between smoking and non-smoking markets. Historically airlines adapted quickly to smoking bans.
